concept.name: Introducing broker
concept.definition: An introducing broker (IB) is a person engaged in soliciting or accepting orders for the purchase or sale of any commodity for future delivery on an exchange who does not accept any money, securities, or property to margin, guarantee, or secure the resulting trades. IBs must register with the CFTC (CEA Section 1a(31)); because they cannot hold customer funds, their customers' accounts are carried by a futures commission merchant.
concept.intuition: An introducing broker is the storefront without the vault: it finds and services futures customers, but their money and positions are actually held by a larger clearing firm (the FCM).
concept.mechanics: The IB markets to and services customers, accepts their orders, and passes the orders and accounts to a carrying FCM under a guarantee or independent IB agreement. The IB earns a share of commissions; all margin and customer funds are handled by the FCM. A securities-industry analogue exists for introducing broker-dealers that clear through carrying firms.
concept.failure_modes: Customers may not realize their assets sit with the FCM, not the IB, so IB marketing failures or misconduct can be misattributed, and the chain complicates accountability. Small IBs can also fail operationally, though customer funds remain at the carrying firm.
concept.misconceptions: An IB is not a lesser FCM — the legal line is precisely that an IB may not touch customer margin funds. 'IB' in retail marketing can also mean a mere referral affiliate, which is a looser usage than the CFTC registration category.
concept.example: A two-person agricultural advisory shop registers as an IB, signs up local farmers for hedging accounts, and all orders and margin are carried and cleared through its partner FCM.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
